Water-drinkers endure cold better than alcohol users, as confirmed by Arctic explorers and trappers. ## Knowledge Graph Community Summaries

The book aims to provide timely, forewarning knowledge to children to influence their life and character.

- Alcohol and Tobacco: Effects on Warmth and Health: Alcohol cannot genuinely warm the body; it causes a false sensation of warmth by drawing blood to the skin, where cold air can carry away more heat, leaving the drinker colder and at greater risk of freezing. Tobacco also weakens the stomach and provides no real help in harsh conditions. Furthermore, spending money on alcohol and tobacco is wasteful and harmful, contributing to sickness, poverty, and crime.

He would push aside the little flap of skin and put into the stomach any kind of food that he pleased, and then watch to see what happened to it. Most of you children are too young to choose what clothes you will wear. Others decide for you. You know, however, that woolen under-garments keep you warm in winter, and that thick boots and stockings should be worn in cold weather. Thin dresses or boots may look pretty; but they are not safe for winter wear, even at a party. A healthy, happy child, dressed in clothes which are suitable for the season, is pleasanter to look at than one whose dress, though rich and handsome, is not warm enough for health or comfort. What you feel, is a muscle (m[)u]s'sl), and it works your joints very much as the rubber strap works the hinge of the door. One end of the muscle is fastened to the bone just below the elbow joint; and the other end, higher up above the joint. When it tightens, or contracts, as we say, it bends the joint. When the arm is straightened, the muscle returns to its first shape. There is another muscle on the outside of the arm which stretches when this one shortens, and so helps the working of the joint. Every joint has two or more muscles of its own to work it. Think how many there must be in our fingers! You can see muscles on the dinner table; for they are only lean meat. [Illustration: _Tendons of the hand._] They are fastened to the bones by strong cords, called tendons (t[)e]n'd[)o]nz). You have all seen the telegraph wires, by which messages are sent from one town to another, all over the country. We will try to learn a little about its wonderful way of working. In your head is your brain. It is the part of you which thinks. If you put your finger on a hot stove, in an instant a message goes on the nerve telegraph to the brain. It tells that wise thinking part that your finger will burn, if it stays on the stove. In another instant, the brain sends back a message to the muscles that move that finger, saying: "Contract quickly, bend the joint, and take that poor finger away so that it will not be burned." You can hardly believe that there was time for all this sending of messages; for as soon as you felt the hot stove, you pulled your finger away. All your food should be eaten slowly and chewed well, so that the saliva may be able to mix with it. Otherwise, the starch may not be changed; and if one part of your body neglects its work, another part will have more than its share to do. That is hardly fair. If you swallow your food in a hurry and do not let the saliva do its work, the stomach will have extra work. But it will find it hard to do more than its own part, and, perhaps, will complain. It can not speak in words; but will by aching, and that is almost as plain as words. SWALLOWING. Next to the chewing, comes the swallowing. Is there any thing wonderful about that? We have two passages leading down our throats. One is to the lungs, for breathing; the other, to the stomach, for swallowing. Do you wonder why the food does not sometimes go down the wrong way? The windpipe leading to the lungs is in front of the other tube. It has at its top a little trap-door. This opens when we breathe and shuts when we swallow, so that the food slips over it safely into the passage behind, which leads to the stomach. If you try to speak while you have food in your mouth, this little door has to open, and some bit of food may slip in. The windpipe will not pass it to the lungs, but tries to force it back. Then we say the food chokes us. If the windpipe can not succeed in forcing back the food, the person will die. HOW THE FOOD IS CARRIED THROUGH THE BODY. But we will suppose that the food of our dinner has gone safely down into the stomach. There the stomach works it over, and mixes in gastric juice, until it is all a gray fluid. Now it is ready to go into the intestines,--a long, coiled tube which leads out of the stomach,--from which the prepared food is taken into the blood. The blood carries it to the heart. - Alcohol and Tobacco: Effects on Warmth and Health: Alcohol cannot genuinely warm the body; it causes a false sensation of warmth by drawing blood to the skin, where cold air can carry away more heat, leaving the drinker colder and at greater risk of freezing. Arctic explorers and hunters confirm that alcohol reduces resistance to cold, and in the Greely expedition, the only former drunkard was the first to die, while tobacco users were more likely to perish. Tobacco also weakens the stomach and provides no real help in harsh conditions. Furthermore, spending money on alcohol and tobacco is wasteful and harmful, contributing to sickness, poverty, and crime.

The Greely expedition illustrates this, as the only former drunkard among the men was the first to die, and most who perished used tobacco, which weakened their ability to survive.

Probably some of you have seen a fire-engine throwing a stream of water through a hose upon a burning building. As the engine forces the water through the hose, so the heart, by the working of its strong muscles, pumps the blood through tubes, shaped like hose, which lead by thousands of little branches all through the body. [Illustration: T]HE blood flows all through the body, carrying good food to every part. It also gathers up from every part the worn-out matter that can no longer be used. By the time it is ready to be sent back by the veins, the blood is no longer pure and red. It is dull and bluish in color, because it is full of impurities. If you look at the veins in your wrist, you will see that they look blue. If all this bad blood goes back to the heart, will the heart have to pump out bad blood next time? No, for the heart has neighbors very near at hand, ready to change the bad blood to pure, red blood again. THE LUNGS. These neighbors are the lungs. They are in the chest on each side of the heart. When you breathe, their little air-cells swell out, or expand, to take in the air. Then they contract again, and the air passes out through your mouth or nose. The lungs must have plenty of fresh air, and plenty of room to work in. [Illustration: _The lungs, heart, and air-passages._] If your clothes are too tight and the lungs do not have room to expand, they can not take in so much air as they should. Then the blood can not be made pure, and the whole body will suffer. For every good breath of fresh air, the lungs take in, they send out one of impure air. In this way, by taking out what is bad, they prepare the blood to go back to the heart pure and red, and to be pumped out through the body again. How the lungs can use the fresh air for doing this good work, you can not yet understand.

Then you might take hold at the other end of the rope and pull as hard and steadily as you could, marking the place to which you raised the weight. By trying this once a week, or once a month, you could tell by the marks, whether you were gaining strength. But how can we gain strength? We must exercise in the open air, and take pure air into our lungs to help purify our blood, and plenty of exercise to make our muscles grow. We must eat good and simple food, that the blood may have supplies to take to every part of the body. ALCOHOL AND STRENGTH. People used to think that alcohol made them strong. Can alcohol make good muscles, or bone, or nerve, or brain? You have already answered "No!" to each of these questions. If it can not make muscles, nor bone nor nerve, nor brain, it can not give you any strength. BEER. Some people may tell you that drinking beer will make you strong. The grain from which the beer is made, would have given you strength. If you should measure your strength before and after drinking beer, you would find that you had not gained any. Most of the food part of the grain has been turned into alcohol. CIDER. The juice of crushed apples, you know, is called cider. As soon as the cider begins to turn sour, or "hard," as people say, alcohol begins to form in it. Pure water is good, and apples are good. But the apple-juice begins to be a poison as soon as there is the least drop of alcohol in it. In cider-making, the alcohol forms in the juice, you know, in a few hours after it is pressed out of the apples. None of the drinks in which there is alcohol, can give you real strength. Then why do people think they can? Because alcohol puts the nerves to sleep, they can not, truly, tell the brain how hard the work is, or how heavy the weight to be lifted. You have all seen the telegraph wires, by which messages are sent from one town to another, all over the country. You are too young to understand how this is done, but you each have something inside of you, by which you are sending messages almost every minute while you are awake. We will try to learn a little about its wonderful way of working. In your head is your brain. It is the part of you which thinks. As you would be very badly off if you could not think, the brain is your most precious part, and you have a strong box made of bone to keep it in. [Illustration: _Diagram of the nervous system._] We will call the brain the central telegraph office. Little white cords, called nerves, connect the brain with the rest of the body. A large cord called the spinal cord, lies safely in a bony case made by the spine, and many nerves branch off from this. If you put your finger on a hot stove, in an instant a message goes on the nerve telegraph to the brain. It tells that wise thinking part that your finger will burn, if it stays on the stove. In another instant, the brain sends back a message to the muscles that move that finger, saying: "Contract quickly, bend the joint, and take that poor finger away so that it will not be burned." You can hardly believe that there was time for all this sending of messages; for as soon as you felt the hot stove, you pulled your finger away. But you really could not have pulled it away, unless the brain had sent word to the muscles to do it. Now, you know what we mean when we say, "As quick as thought." Surely nothing could be quicker. You see that the brain has a great deal of work to do, for it has to send so many orders. You do not have to think about breathing, and yet the muscles work all the time, moving your chest. The text details several specific harmful effects of alcohol on the human body:

1. **On the brain and nerves:** Alcohol in the blood goes to the brain, where it affects the nerves and makes a person lose control over his actions. It injures the brain and nerves so they cannot work well or send their messages properly, which is why a drunkard "does not know what he is about." It puts the nerves to sleep, making people careless and unable to tell the difference between a railroad track and a place of safety.

2. **On the blood:** Good blood is made from good food, but it "can not be good if it has been poisoned with alcohol." Alcohol in the blood is described as a poison.

3. **On the muscles and heart:** Since the heart is made of muscle, alcohol does the same harm to it as to other muscles. Alcohol can make the heart fatty, and a fatty heart cannot work as well as a muscular one. Alcohol also makes the heart beat too fast, so it gets too tired.

4. **On the senses:** A person in the habit of using alcoholic drinks cannot touch, taste, see, smell, or hear as well as he ought. His hands tremble, his speech is sometimes thick, he often cannot walk straight, and he may think he sees things that are not there because his nerves are confused.

5. **On body warmth:** Alcohol gives only a false sensation of warmth by drawing blood to the skin, where cold air carries away more heat, leaving the drinker colder and at greater risk of freezing.

6. **General effects:** Even a little alcohol makes the head ache and hurts the brain and nerves, and people who drink a little regularly slowly poison their bodies, making them less able to bear sickness and less likely to recover.

generated_answer:
The text says candy is a form of sugar that most children like so much they risk eating more sugar than is good for them, and that pure candy should be made only of sugar (it will dissolve completely in water, like sugar does). However, candy-makers sometimes substitute cheaper white earth (chalk) for sugar, which is not good food.

As for how sugar becomes alcohol: the text explains that ripe grape juice contains water and sugar. When the juice is left standing in a warm place, the sugar changes into alcohol and a gas (carbonic acid gas) that bubbles off. This changed juice is called wine. A similar process happens with barley: its starch is turned into sugar (making malt), and then yeast is added to change the sugar into gas and alcohol, producing beer. In both cases, the sugar is transformed into alcohol and a gas.
gold_answer: Candy contains sugar, and sugar is changed into alcohol.

Take two little bones, such as those from the legs or wings of a chicken, put one of them into the fire, when it is not very hot, and leave it there two or three hours. Soak the other bone in some weak muriatic (m[=u] r[)i] [)a]t'[)i]k) acid. This acid can be bought of any druggist. You will have to be careful in taking the bone out of the fire, for it is all ready to break. If you strike it a quick blow, it will crumble to dust. This dust we call lime, and it is very much like the lime from which the mason makes mortar. [Illustration: _Bone tied to a knot._] The acid has taken the lime from the other bone, so only the part which is not lime is left. You will be surprised to see how easily it will bend. You can twist it and tie it into a knot; but it will not easily break. You have seen gristle in meat. This soft part of the bone is gristle. Children's bones have more gristle than those of older people; so children's bones bend easily. I know a lady who has one leg shorter than the other. This makes her lame, and she has to wear a boot with iron supports three or four inches high, in order to walk at all. One day she told me how she became lame. "I remember," she said, "when I was between three and four years old, sitting one day in my high chair at the table, and twisting one foot under the little step of the chair. The next morning I felt lame; but nobody could tell what was the matter. At last, the doctors found out that the trouble all came from that twist. It had gone too far to be cured. Before I had this boot, I could only walk with a crutch." CARE OF THE SPINE. Because the spine is made of little bones with cushions between them, it bends easily, and children sometimes bend it more than they ought. If you lean over your book or your writing or any other work, the elastic cushions may get so pressed on the inner edge that they do not easily spring back into shape. In this way, you may grow round-shouldered or hump-backed. This bending over, also cramps the lungs, so that they do not have all the room they need for breathing. While you are young, your bones are easily bent. One shoulder or one hip gets higher than the other, if you stand unevenly. - Alcohol and Tobacco: Effects on Warmth and Health: Alcohol cannot genuinely warm the body; it causes a false sensation of warmth by drawing blood to the skin, where cold air can carry away more heat, leaving the drinker colder and at greater risk of freezing. Arctic explorers and hunters confirm that alcohol reduces resistance to cold, and in the Greely expedition, the only former drunkard was the first to die, while tobacco users were more likely to perish. Tobacco also weakens the stomach and provides no real help in harsh conditions. It is part of the Pathfinder Series and endorsed by the Women's Christian Temperance Union. The book aims to provide timely and forewarning knowledge to children about these substances, as required by laws in several states, including Massachusetts. It is designed to be simple and practical for young students.

- Alcohol's Deceptive Effect on Cold: Alcohol creates a false feeling of warmth by drawing blood to the skin, but this actually accelerates heat loss, making the drinker colder and impairing their judgment, which can lead to freezing. Water-drinkers endure cold better than alcohol users, as confirmed by Arctic explorers and trappers. A soldier was once shot in the side in such a way that when the wound healed, it left an opening with a piece of loose skin over it, like a little door leading into his stomach. A doctor who wished to learn about the stomach, hired him for a servant and used to study him every day. He would push aside the little flap of skin and put into the stomach any kind of food that he pleased, and then watch to see what happened to it. In this way, he learned a great deal and wrote it down, so that other people might know, too. In other ways, also, which it would take too long to tell you here, doctors have learned how these magical food-bags take care of our food. WHY DOES THE FOOD NEED TO BE CHANGED? Your mamma tells you sometimes at breakfast that you must eat oat-meal and milk to make you grow into a big man or woman. Did you ever wonder what part of you is made of oat-meal, or what part of milk? That stout little arm does not look like oat-meal; those rosy cheeks do not look like milk. If our food is to make stout arms and rosy cheeks, strong bodies and busy brains, it must first be changed into a form in which it can get to each part and feed it. **Body's Organs Work Together as a 'Busy Workshop' to Keep People Healthy**

Health experts describe the human body as a "busy work-shop" where many kinds of work are carried out all day and all night. Even while we lie still and sleep, the breathing must go on, as must the work of those other organs that never stop until we die.

At the center of this operation is the brain. One part of the brain has to take care of all the rest of the body and keep every organ at work; it can never go to sleep itself. If it did, the heart would stop pumping, the lungs would leave off breathing, and the body would be dead. Another part of the brain does the thinking, and this part needs rest. Experts warn that if the thinking part does not get good, quiet sleep, it will soon wear out, and a worn-out brain is not easy to repair.

The nerves act as delicate little messengers. Each kind of message travels on its own thread, so the messages never get mixed or confused. They do all the feeling for the whole body, giving us many pains and many pleasures. If there were no nerves in your hands, you might cut them and feel no pain, but you also could not feel a mother's soft, warm hand. The nerves are easily tired out and need much rest; they get rested by a change of work.

Meanwhile, the stomach plays a vital role in feeding the body. One way to take care of the stomach is to give it only its own work to do. The teeth must first do their work faithfully, and the stomach must have rest. It cannot work well unless it is quite warm. If a person pours ice-water into the stomach as he eats, the work stops until the stomach gets warm again.

The skin also does essential work. Tiny holes called pores are the mouths of tiny tubes that carry off waste matter and water from the body. Pieced together, all the perspiration tubes in the skin of one person would make a line more than three miles long. This waste matter is always coming out through the skin, both in winter and summer. Health officials stress that the body is kept healthy by having its worn-out matter carried off in this way. If the skin could not do its work, a person would die.

Authorities warn, however, that certain substances can disrupt this delicate teamwork. Any drink that contains alcohol is not a food to make one strong; it is a poison that injures the brain and nerves so they cannot send their messages properly. Alcohol also injures the gastric juice so it cannot mix with food, and can cause sores on the delicate lining of the stomach. When the nerves are put to sleep by alcohol, people become careless and do not do their work faithfully.

Tobacco, too, harms the system. It makes the mouth very dry, discolors the teeth, makes bad sores in the mouth, and often causes disease of the throat. It deadens the nerves so a person does not feel the cold or take pains to keep warm, and it puts the nerves to sleep very much as alcohol does.

In short, every part of the body depends on every other part. No part can fail to do its work without causing trouble to the rest of the body. Experts advise that the least we can do is to take care of these organs and keep them in good order, so the whole body can work together to keep us well and happy.
gold_answer: Science News — The human body relies on a coordinated system of organs to maintain health. Food is essential for the body and is needed by the brain. The stomach produces gastric juice to digest food, while blood carries nutrients to the heart. The heart, made of muscles, pumps blood to the lungs, which are located in the chest. Nerves help muscles know when to move, and bones give structure through the spine. This teamwork keeps the body functioning properly.
